extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, law students, and practitioners advising on patent assignments and licenses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on defenses available to assignees against assignors and on rights/remedies of licensees and licensors (specific performance, rescission, damages, recovery of payments), including effects of statutory requirements for negotiable notes. Focuses on U.S. patent assignment and licensing disputes and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of patent invalidity defence by contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's right to defend against an action for purchase money on the ground that the patent is void may be waived by the parties in their contract, and where they have expressly provided another manner for possible invalidity, the assignee cannot allege it as an answer to the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the conveyance/contract contains provisions allocating risk of invalidity, those contractual provisions govern rather than an assignee's otherwise-available defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of earlier patents as defence (assignee ignorant at purchase)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the invention covered by the patent is an infringement upon earlier patents has been declared to be a defence if the assignee was ignorant of this fact at the time of purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, the grant of a later patent for the same invention offers no bar to recovery by the assignor; the defense depends on prior-existing rights and the assignee's knowledge at purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent representations by assignor as defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraudulent representations by the assignor that led the assignee to purchase the monopoly constitute a defence to an action for the purchase price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such representations must be averments of existing facts (not mere opinion or puffing) and may relate to title, validity, utility or value. The assignee, defending on this ground, must offer to return the patent and show he derived no benefits therefrom or render an account of benefits received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of evidence of prior patent invalidating a note action
rubrics_metrics.description: In a suit on a note given for a patent-right, evidence that the patent was void as being an infringement of a prior patent is not admissible unless that fact has been found by a competent Federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court will generally require a competent adjudication of the invalidity/infringement before allowing such evidence in an action on a note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of warranty as entire or partial defence
rubrics_metrics.description: A breach of warranty may constitute an entire or partial defence to an action for the purchase money, depending on the nature of the covenant broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied warranty of title and express warranty of validity are of the essence; breach relieves assignee from obligations. Other covenants' effects depend on how much their non-fulfilment impairs the patent's value. If breach equals total failure of consideration or price cannot be apportioned, assignor's action fails; otherwise, apportionment may be ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory form requirements and negotiable notes given for patents
rubrics_metrics.description: State statutes may require notes given for patents to recite that they are for a patent, putting subsequent holders on inquiry as to consideration; such statutes aim to protect assignees from fraudsters negotiating notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a note properly discloses it is for a patent, a holder can be subject to any defenses that could have been advanced against the assignor. Omitting the notice may make negotiable paper open to defences in some States, especially where the subsequent holder had notice of the consideration or of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bona fide holder rule for negotiable paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the law merchant, negotiable paper in the hands of a bona fide holder who took it in the usual course of business before maturity is good against the maker, irrespective of equities or defences between maker and assignor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraud in procuring the note is not a defense against a bona fide holder. State statutes that require specific statements on notes may alter inquiry duties of subsequent holders, but an innocent holder generally may rely on notes in ordinary form.

rubrics_metrics.name: State power to regulate sale/form but not to impair patent franchise
rubrics_metrics.description: States may prescribe forms for contracts or regulate the use or sale of patented articles, and require filings (e.g., copies of letters-patent), but statutes limiting the right to sell patent privileges themselves have been held unconstitutional as impairing franchises conferred by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes imposing procedural requirements (e.g., notice on notes) are generally upheld; substantive impairment of patent franchise may be invalid under federal constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee's duty to return patent or account when asserting fraud defence
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee asserting fraud in the sale must offer to return the patent and show that he derived no benefits therefrom, or must render an account of any benefits received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is necessary to avoid unjust enrichment where the assignee seeks to avoid payment after obtaining value from the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal right of licensee to enjoy licensed privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: The only universal right of licensees against licensors is the enjoyment of the privileges conferred by the license, free from assertion of the patentee's prohibitory powers against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other licensee rights arise from the particular contracts they enter and must be analyzed under those contractual terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available remedies to licensee enumerated
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal remedies for wrongs by licensors are four: (1) specific performance of the contract; (2) rescission of the contract; (3) an action for damages; and (4) an action to recover back money improperly paid to the licensor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise groups licensee wrongs under the remedy appropriate to redress them; choice of remedy depends on the nature of the licensor's breach or misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific performance and injunctions for licensees
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity will decree specific performance of license contracts or enjoin conduct contrary to rights conferred by the license where licensor refuses essential instruments, agreed-to fee reductions are violated, or licensor invades the license (forfeiture declarations, warning public, licensing others contrary to exclusivity, threatening to retire and assign patent to destroy value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity considers circumstances and potential irreparable injury; injunctions may be granted when damages are not readily ascertainable or would not adequately compensate loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses are personal; equitable interference limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The license contract is fundamentally personal; if no ground for equitable interference exists in the subject-matter or irreparable injury, the licensee must seek remedies at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not supply specific performance absent the personal/contractual or irreparable-injury predicates that justify equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescission of license for fraud or flagrant breach
rubrics_metrics.description: A license and its dependent contracts may be rescinded in equity for fraudulent representations by the licensor inducing acceptance, or for flagrant breaches that prevent the licensee from enjoying the licensed privileges (including successful injunctions against licensee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rescission formally cancels the license and makes the licensee a stranger to the patent going forward; equitable considerations govern whether rescission is proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action for damages by licensee for breach of contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee may maintain an action at law for damages for any breach of the license contract; violation of exclusivity or covenants not to license others renders licensor liable for resulting injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts by the licensor that operate as recognition of privileges in others (suits, concessions, or licensing) may constitute breaches; licensee may elect remedies including damages or equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor's covenant to sue infringers and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Where licensor agrees to sue infringers and use due diligence to protect licensee, licensor is liable if he neglects that duty, but such covenant does not obligate him to attack claims based on adverse patents or estop him from asserting his patent's invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promises to prosecute may create contractual duties; but they do not convert licenses into warranties of validity vis-à-vis third-party adverse claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of license fees paid by mistake or fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: An action will lie to recover license fees paid by mistake or procured by the licensor's fraud; where multiple patents are licensed and some have expired, apportionment and refund for expired patents may be ordered if payment was in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensee derived equivalent benefits from the license, restitution may be denied (only nominal damages recoverable). A later adjudication that a patent is invalid alone is not a ground for recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor's rights governed by private contract; usual remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensor's rights against licensee are governed by their private contract and can take any agreed form; rescission in equity is rare, with actions for damages and unpaid fees being the common remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because license terms define obligations, enforcement is generally contractual rather than sui generis equitable except in cases of serious misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescission by licensor for licensee misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensor may obtain rescission of a license in equity where the licensee's misconduct renders continuance prejudicial (e.g., assignment of a purely personal license, or failure to manufacture and sell as required so as to abandon the license).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rescission is not automatic; a mere notice to cease does not annul the license. The licensee has a right to be heard before forfeiture is declared, and equitable relief may be conditioned on the licensor having substantially fulfilled his covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action for breach of contract or infringement by licensor
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensor may sue a licensee for breach of contract; if the licensee's wrongful acts also constitute patent infringement, the licensor may elect to pursue either contract damages or infringement remedies (measure of contract damages is the injury caused by the infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of remedy affects damages calculation and available relief; jurisdictional considerations (e.g., federal courts for infringement) may also determine the forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-payment of royalties and forfeiture rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is not ipso facto forfeited by non-payment of royalties unless the license so provides; the licensor's remedies for unpaid royalties are ordinarily at law, and may be constrained as to forum (e.g., local courts for royalties vs. federal courts for infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should specify forfeiture conditions in the license; absent such provisions equity will not generally annul the license for mere non-payment without following contractual or legal procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceeding license scope constitutes infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a licensee uses the patented invention beyond the limits of the license or in an unauthorized way, that violation constitutes an infringement of the patentee's exclusive rights (subject to jurisdictional and party-capacity rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where covenants within the license are performed, acts beyond the license's scope may be actionable under federal patent law (infringement) as well as under contract theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint licensors and necessity of joining parties for relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Where multiple joint licensors exist and the licensee seeks a change of license terms, all joint licensors must be made parties for a decree to change the terms to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable relief altering multi-party contractual arrangements requires bringing in all interested parties to bind rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will not aid a licensor in default of his covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity will not enforce a licensor's rights (e.g., to rescind or obtain specific performance) if the licensor has not substantially fulfilled his own obligations under the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee may set off or defend on grounds that would have been available in a suit at law for infringement; courts balance mutual performance when considering equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for injunctive relief (irreparable injury and ascertainability of damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be granted when the licensor's conduct threatens irreparable injury (e.g., public declarations of forfeiture that would destroy business confidence) and damages would not be readily ascertainable or adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider public confidence, difficulty of valuing harm, and whether monetary relief would be adequate in deciding injunctive relief for licensees.
